paper.title: Difficulty Calibration Across Time for Membership Inference in Diffusion Models
paper.abstract:
Abstract Modern diffusion models are trained on massive datasets that often include copyrighted or private images. Membership inference attacks (MIAs) address this by testing whether a given image was in a model’s training set. The standard approach scores an image by its reconstruction loss and flags low-loss images as members. This often fails because some images are simply easier to reconstruct than others, so a simple unseen image can score a lower loss than a complex training image. Difficulty calibration separates memorization from how difficult an image is to begin with. We show how to calibrate along two axes of time: training time and diffusion time. First, across training time, we introduce Reference-Model Calibration (RMC), which compares a fine-tuned model’s loss against an earlier checkpoint. This cleanly isolates newly memorized data and gives near-perfect auditing, even without text captions. Since earlier checkpoints are not always available, we next present Temporal Self-Calibration (TSC), which calibrates across diffusion time using only a single model. Our key observation is that an image’s difficulty persists across noise levels, whereas memorization is localized in time. By comparing the loss at a target timestep against neighboring timesteps from the same model, TSC attenuates image difficulty using the model’s own trajectory. Empirically, our methods beat the state of the art by a wide margin, and unlike most existing attacks, generalize across different model parameterizations such as x x -, v v -, and ϵ \epsilon -prediction models.
Code is available at https://github.com/MichaelJoseph777/TSC .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion Models (DMs) ( Song and Ermon, 2019 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2020 ) are currently the method of choice for high-fidelity image generation ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Ramesh et al., 2022 ) . As their success relies heavily on massive, uncurated web-scale datasets, these models often inadvertently absorb personal photographs, copyrighted artworks, and proprietary content. This indiscriminate data collection creates privacy and copyright risks, with recent studies ( Carlini et al., 2023 ; Somepalli et al., 2023 ) demonstrating that DMs can memorize and reproduce specific training examples during generation. Consequently, it has become increasingly important to reliably audit the underlying training corpora of these generative models. Membership Inference Attacks (MIAs) ( Shokri et al., 2017 ) audit this risk by predicting whether a specific sample was part of the training set. While typically framed as a security vulnerability, MIAs can also enable creators to verify whether their proprietary content was used for training. These attacks exploit statistical differences in model behavior on members versus non-members ( Yeom et al., 2018 ) . Although well-studied for earlier generative models such as GANs ( Goodfellow et al., 2020 ) and VAEs ( Kingma and Welling, 2013 ) , with several attacks developed for these settings ( Hayes et al., 2017 ; Hilprecht et al., 2019 ; Chen et al., 2020 ) , the iterative denoising process of diffusion models makes traditional MIAs considerably less effective ( Duan et al., 2023 ) , motivating approaches tailored specifically to the diffusion process. Probably the most standard approach to MIAs is evaluating the models loss on the target examples, and predicting the low loss examples as members. Early approaches applied this to DMs by directly measuring the reconstruction error at a single, isolated timestep ( Matsumoto et al., 2023 ) . While followup work improved upon this ( Duan et al., 2023 ; Kong et al., 2024 ) , a fundamental obstacle limits the accuracy of all these approaches: There are images that are intrinsically easy that achieve low loss regardless of membership and vice versa. This difficulty factor confounds membership making the loss an unreliable membership metric. To overcome this confound, we propose difficulty calibration across two time axes: training time and diffusion time . First, across training time, we introduce Reference-Model Calibration (RMC) to audit fine-tuned models. By comparing a sample’s fine-tuned loss against the base checkpoint loss, RMC cleanly isolates newly memorized data from general reconstruction difficult. Note that this strategy is known for Large Language Models ( Wang et al., 2024 ) but is under-explored in DMs. Its limitation is that prior checkpoints are frequently unavailable, and the approach is irrelevant for pretraining corpora. To provide an unconstrained alternative, we propose Temporal Self-Calibration (TSC) , which calibrates across diffusion time using only a single model. TSC leverages the insight that image difficulty persists across nearby noise levels, whereas the membership signal is highly localized in time. By evaluating the relative loss differences between a target timestep and its temporal neighbors, TSC uses the local trajectory as an internal baseline to suppress difficulty-induced variance. This internal calibration isolates the structural deviation of membership, successfully identifying a ”difficult” member even when its absolute loss strictly exceeds that of an ”easy” non-member. We evaluate our methods across multiple model architectures, datasets, and training targets. While RMC provides state-of-the-art auditing for fine-tuned Stable Diffusion models, TSC serves as a highly powerful alternative for unconstrained settings. Across DDPM and Stable Diffusion evaluation settings, TSC consistently outperforms prior baselines. On CIFAR-10 ( Krizhevsky et al., 2009 ) , it doubles the performance of existing attacks to reach a 62.3% TPR@1%FPR. Furthermore, we emphasize TSC’s robustness across diverse training objectives. While existing attacks are rigidly tailored to standard noise-prediction models and severely degrade on alternative parameterizations, TSC maintains highly accurate extraction capabilities. Finally, we analyze where the membership signal physically appears along the denoising trajectory, demonstrating that the effective leakage window is intrinsically tied to the underlying training objective. Our contributions are: • We propose TSC , a generalized method for robust membership inference. By evaluating relative loss differences across adjacent timesteps, TSC uses the local trajectory as an internal baseline to mitigate image difficulty and isolate membership signal. • We introduce RMC for auditing fine-tuned models. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to systematically analyze and demonstrate the effectiveness of prior-checkpoint calibration of single-timestep losses for membership inference in diffusion models. • We comprehensively evaluate both methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance across diverse architectures and datasets. Notably, TSC consistently yields massive improvements over prior trajectory-based baselines, frequently doubling the true positive rate at strict false-positive thresholds. • We provide a detailed analysis of how the effective denoising timesteps for membership inference shift across different training objectives, extending robust membership inference beyond the standard ϵ \epsilon -prediction, ϵ \epsilon -loss paradigm.

sections.heading: Membership inference attacks.
sections.text: Membership inference attacks (MIAs), originally formalized by Shokri et al. (2017) , aim to determine whether a specific data record was included in a target model’s training set. MIAs are traditionally categorized by the adversary’s capabilities: white-box attacks assume access to model parameters, activations, or gradients ( Nasr et al., 2019 ) , whereas black-box attacks operate under a more restrictive setting, relying exclusively on the model’s observable outputs ( Choquette-Choo et al., 2021 ) . Gray-box attacks occupy an intermediate threat model, granting access to quantities such as loss values or intermediate model states without requiring gradient-level information. In diffusion-model auditing, this distinction is often methodological: attacks that query intermediate denoising states generally assume local access to the model while avoiding the substantially greater computational cost of full white-box analysis. Most such query-based MIAs are threshold-based attacks : they define a continuous membership score 𝒮 θ ​ ( x ) \mathcal{S}_{\theta}(x) , such as reconstruction loss or prediction error, for a target model θ \theta and candidate sample x x , and classify the sample as a member when 𝒮 θ ​ ( x ) < τ {\mathcal{S}_{\theta}(x)<\tau} ( Yeom et al., 2018 ; Carlini et al., 2022 ) . The threshold τ \tau can be empirically calibrated to optimize attack performance, often subject to a desired False Positive Rate (FPR). More sophisticated attacks additionally use shadow models to calibrate the score distribution ( Shokri et al., 2017 ; Carlini et al., 2022 ) .

sections.heading: MIAs on diffusion models.
sections.text: Auditing diffusion models requires analyzing the iterative denoising trajectory. While Carlini et al. (2022) achieved high precision with the Likelihood Ratio Attack (LiRA), their approach requires training numerous shadow models, making it computationally prohibitive. Consequently, efficient threshold-based attacks have become the standard. Matsumoto et al. (2023) introduced the Naive loss attack, which utilizes the diffusion training loss at specific timesteps as the membership score. To extract a more robust signal, Duan et al. (2023) proposed SecMI, which evaluates the reconstruction error along a deterministic trajectory via DDIM inversion, effectively isolating the membership signal from the high variance of stochastic forward noise. Kong et al. (2024) introduced the Proximal Initialization Attack (PIA), which initializes the forward process with a known deterministic noise vector near the clean data sample. PIA infers membership by evaluating the model’s noise estimation against this explicit ground-truth trajectory, achieving competitive accuracy with a reduced query budget. Finally, for conditional text-to-image models, Zhai et al. (2024) proposed CLiD, which measures the discrepancy between conditional and unconditional diffusion losses to expose memorization specific to the text-image pair.

sections.heading: Calibration across training time.
sections.text: For models fine-tuned from a foundational base checkpoint, the original model provides a natural reference across training time . It establishes an accurate baseline of each image’s difficulty before the audited fine-tuning stage. As shown for Stable Diffusion on MS-COCO ( Lin et al., 2014 ) (Fig. 2 ), the losses produced by the two checkpoints are highly correlated. However, subtracting the pretrained loss to compute the fine-tuning residual reveals a stark separation: members systematically shift toward lower fine-tuned loss, while non-members remain concentrated near zero. Table 1 demonstrates the empirical strength of this baseline against CLiD. By isolating the loss residual and thereby neutralizing image difficulty, a minimal two-query, uncaptioned reference evaluation heavily outperforms a 15-query, fully captioned, CLiD attack. Expanding to a comparable 20-query budget yields near-perfect auditing across all datasets. These results demonstrate that separating the membership signal from baseline difficulty is crucial for strict low-FPR auditing, directly motivating our reference-free temporal approach. sections.heading: Calibration across diffusion time.
sections.text: While a pretrained checkpoint provides an exceptionally strong baseline, assuming access to one is often unrealistic and irrelevant for auditing pretraining corpus. To achieve difficulty calibration without privileged external models, our primary method instead calibrates across diffusion time , leveraging the denoising trajectory itself as a self-contained internal reference. Because image difficulty generally evolves smoothly across nearby noise levels, adjacent timesteps provide an image-specific estimate of the local loss baseline. sections.heading: Models and datasets.
sections.text: For standard image synthesis, we evaluate DDPMs ( Ho et al., 2020 ) on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 ( Krizhevsky et al., 2009 ) , STL-10-U ( Coates et al., 2011 ) , and Tiny ImageNet ( Deng et al., 2009 ) , as well as DDPM++ backbone ( Song et al., 2020 ) on CIFAR-100. For text-to-image generation, we evaluate Stable Diffusion v1.4 ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) fine-tuned on the Pokémon ( Pinkney, 2022 ) , MS-COCO ( Lin et al., 2014 ) , and Flickr30k ( Young et al., 2014 ) datasets. Complete model configurations and dataset splits are detailed in Appendix B .

sections.heading: Baselines and evaluation metrics.
sections.text: We compare TSC against established MIAs for DMs: Naive ( Matsumoto et al., 2023 ) , SecMI ( Duan et al., 2023 ) , PIA, and PIAN ( Kong et al., 2024 ) . We measure performance across all methods using Attack Success Rate (ASR), AUC, and True Positive Rate at 1% False Positive Rate (TPR@1%FPR).

sections.heading: Implementation details.
sections.text: Hyperparameters for both TSC (the optimal center λ ⋆ \lambda^{\star} ) and timestep-dependent baselines (Naive, PIA) are tuned by maximizing AUC on a disjoint shadow data split. As analyzed in our results, these optimal coordinates naturally shift depending on the model’s loss weighting. For TSC, we fix the temporal window at 2 ​ Δ = 5 2\Delta=5 log-SNR. λ ∗ \lambda^{*} is fixed at 0.75 0.75 for DDPM benchmarks and 0.25 0.25 for SD trained models. To balance efficiency, we allocate a proportionate query budget that ensures stable evaluation. However, as shown in Fig. 5 , the attack performance can improve further with higher query budget.

TSC consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance across all datasets. While it provides solid improvements in overall AUC and ASR, its most significant advantage emerges in the high-confidence regime. On CIFAR-10, TSC achieves a TPR@1%FPR of 62.31%, doubling the performance of the strongest baseline (PIAN at 30.90%). For text-to-image models (Table 3 ), we evaluate Stable Diffusion under a realistic uncaptioned threat model. Because training prompts are typically unknown to an auditor, omitting ground-truth captions prevents artificially inflating attack success via prompt-specific overfitting, directly isolating the inherent image-level membership signal. Under this setting, TSC outperforms all baselines across every metric on MS-COCO and Flickr30k. The exception is the Pokémon fine-tune, where PIA prevails. We attribute this to the dataset’s limited scale and visual uniformity. Such low diversity naturally minimizes the variance in image difficulty, allowing PIA’s proximal measurement to perform exceptionally well without requiring relative calibration. By evaluating PIA at these tuned coordinates, our reported baselines are notably stronger than standard static evaluations.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced difficulty calibration across two time axes to mitigate the image-difficulty confound in diffusion MIAs. Reference-Model Calibration (RMC) calibrates across training time using a pretrained checkpoint, while Temporal Self-Calibration (TSC) calibrates across diffusion time using the image’s own denoising trajectory. Experiments across diverse datasets, architectures, and training objectives demonstrate substantial gains in strict low-FPR membership detection. RMC enables near-perfect uncaptioned auditing of fine-tuned data, and TSC frequently doubles the TPR@1%FPR of the strongest trajectory-based baselines in fully unconstrained settings.

sections.heading: Limitations and future work.
sections.text: Although our methods use only forward predictions and do not require gradients, they assume access to denoising outputs for candidate images at selected noise levels. This access may be unavailable through APIs that expose only final generated images, limiting direct application in such settings. RMC additionally assumes access to the checkpoint from which the audited model was fine-tuned. Its applicability is therefore restricted when this checkpoint is unavailable or the model’s training lineage is unknown. Future work could investigate whether related public checkpoints or ensembles of reference models can provide effective difficulty calibration in these cases. RMC measures loss changes between checkpoints and does not separately identify membership in the reference model’s pretraining corpus. Studying overlap between pretraining and fine-tuning data, and extending calibration across successive checkpoints, could clarify how membership evidence evolves across training stages.

sections.heading: Ethics statement
sections.text: Membership inference has both privacy risks and legitimate auditing uses. Improved attacks could be misused to infer an individual’s participation in sensitive training data. At the same time, these methods can help individuals investigate whether their personal data were used to train or fine-tune diffusion models, and can support audits of candidate training-data sources for publicly released models, including those distributed through platforms such as Hugging Face. Such audits can help assess claims about dataset use and improve transparency around model provenance. Membership scores provide statistical evidence about candidate examples: a negative result does not prove that an example was excluded from training, and an audit does not identify a model’s complete training dataset. We advocate using these methods for authorized privacy auditing and accountability, with conclusions that account for false positives and false negatives.

sections.heading: Scope of the explanation.
sections.text: The benefit of symmetry depends on the removed odd variation being primarily nuisance and on the centered contrast retaining membership information. An odd membership component would also be removed, and sample-dependent even variation remains. Symmetry is therefore a useful invariance, not a universal optimality claim or a guarantee that all image difficulty is eliminated. In particular, smoothness of difficulty alone does not ensure its cancellation over a wide window. This account is compatible with a broad membership feature and does not identify a unique latent difficulty factor from observed losses. These statements refer to symmetry in the evaluated log-SNR coordinates. Mapping requested levels to a discrete diffusion schedule can yield slightly unequal realized distances. In that case, a a and b b in Eq. equation 12 should be computed from the realized coordinate. Nominally equal spacing alone does not imply exact odd-component cancellation.

Membership inference attacks (MIAs) address this by testing whether a given image was in a model’s training set. The standard approach scores an image by its reconstruction loss and flags low-loss images as members. This often fails because some images are simply easier to reconstruct than others, so a simple unseen image can score a lower loss than a complex training image. Difficulty calibration separates memorization from how difficult an image is to begin with. We show how to calibrate along two axes of time: training time and diffusion time. First, across training time, we introduce Reference-Model Calibration (RMC), which compares a fine-tuned model’s loss against an earlier checkpoint. This cleanly isolates newly memorized data and gives near-perfect auditing, even without text captions. Since earlier checkpoints are not always available, we next present Temporal Self-Calibration (TSC), which calibrates across diffusion time using only a single model. Our key observation is that an image’s difficulty persists across noise levels, whereas memorization is localized in time. By comparing the loss at a target timestep against neighboring timesteps from the same model, TSC attenuates image difficulty using the model’s own trajectory. Empirically, our methods beat the state of the art by a wide margin, and unlike most existing attacks, generalize across different model parameterizations such as x x -, v v -, and ϵ \epsilon -prediction models. Code is available at https://github.com/MichaelJoseph777/TSC . 1 Introduction Diffusion Models (DMs) ( Song and Ermon, 2019 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2020 ) are currently the method of choice for high-fidelity image generation ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Ramesh et al., 2022 ) . As their success relies heavily on massive, uncurated web-scale datasets, these models often inadvertently absorb personal photographs, copyrighted artworks, and proprietary content. This indiscriminate data collection creates privacy and copyright risks, with recent studies ( Carlini et al., 2023 ; Somepalli et al., 2023 ) demonstrating that DMs can memorize and reproduce specific training examples during generation. Consequently, it has become increasingly important to reliably audit the underlying training corpora of these generative models. Membership Inference Attacks (MIAs) ( Shokri et al., 2017 ) audit this risk by predicting whether a specific sample was part of the training set. While typically framed as a security vulnerability, MIAs can also enable creators to verify whether their proprietary content was used for training. These attacks exploit statistical differences in model behavior on members versus non-members ( Yeom et al., 2018 ) . Although well-studied for earlier generative models such as GANs ( Goodfellow et al., 2020 ) and VAEs ( Kingma and Welling, 2013 ) , with several attacks developed for these settings ( Hayes et al., 2017 ; Hilprecht et al., 2019 ; Chen et al., 2020 ) , the iterative denoising process of diffusion models makes traditional MIAs considerably less effective ( Duan et al., 2023 ) , motivating approaches tailored specifically to the diffusion process. Probably the most standard approach to MIAs is evaluating the models loss on the target examples, and predicting the low loss examples as members. Early approaches applied this to DMs by directly measuring the reconstruction error at a single, isolated timestep ( Matsumoto et al., 2023 ) . While followup work improved upon this ( Duan et al., 2023 ; Kong et al., 2024 ) , a fundamental obstacle limits the accuracy of all these approaches: There are images that are intrinsically easy that achieve low loss regardless of membership and vice versa. This difficulty factor confounds membership making the loss an unreliable membership metric. To overcome this confound, we propose difficulty calibration across two time axes: training time and diffusion time . First, across training time, we introduce Reference-Model Calibration (RMC) to audit fine-tuned models. By comparing a sample’s fine-tuned loss against the base checkpoint loss, RMC cleanly isolates newly memorized data from general reconstruction difficult. Note that this strategy is known for Large Language Models ( Wang et al., 2024 ) but is under-explored in DMs. Its limitation is that prior checkpoints are frequently unavailable, and the approach is irrelevant for pretraining corpora. To provide an unconstrained alternative, we propose Temporal Self-Calibration (TSC) , which calibrates across diffusion time using only a single model. TSC leverages the insight that image difficulty persists across nearby noise levels, whereas the membership signal is highly localized in time. By evaluating the relative loss differences between a target timestep and its temporal neighbors, TSC uses the local trajectory as an internal baseline to suppress difficulty-induced variance. This internal calibration isolates the structural deviation of membership, successfully identifying a ”difficult” member even when its absolute loss strictly exceeds that of an ”easy” non-member. We evaluate our methods across multiple model architectures, datasets, and training targets. While RMC provides state-of-the-art auditing for fine-tuned Stable Diffusion models, TSC serves as a highly powerful alternative for unconstrained settings. Across DDPM and Stable Diffusion evaluation settings, TSC consistently outperforms prior baselines. On CIFAR-10 ( Krizhevsky et al., 2009 ) , it doubles the performance of existing attacks to reach a 62.3% TPR@1%FPR. Furthermore, we emphasize TSC’s robustness across diverse training objectives. While existing attacks are rigidly tailored to standard noise-prediction models and severely degrade on alternative parameterizations, TSC maintains highly accurate extraction capabilities. Finally, we analyze where the membership signal physically appears along the denoising trajectory, demonstrating that the effective leakage window is intrinsically tied to the underlying training objective. Our contributions are: • We propose TSC , a generalized method for robust membership inference. By evaluating relative loss differences across adjacent timesteps, TSC uses the local trajectory as an internal baseline to mitigate image difficulty and isolate membership signal. • We introduce RMC for auditing fine-tuned models. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to systematically analyze and demonstrate the effectiveness of prior-checkpoint calibration of single-timestep losses for membership inference in diffusion models. • We comprehensively evaluate both methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance across diverse architectures and datasets. Notably, TSC consistently yields massive improvements over prior trajectory-based baselines, frequently doubling the true positive rate at strict false-positive thresholds. • We provide a detailed analysis of how the effective denoising timesteps for membership inference shift across different training objectives, extending robust membership inference beyond the standard ϵ \epsilon -prediction, ϵ \epsilon -loss paradigm. 2 Related Work Membership inference attacks. Membership inference attacks (MIAs), originally formalized by Shokri et al. (2017) , aim to determine whether a specific data record was included in a target model’s training set. MIAs are traditionally categorized by the adversary’s capabilities: white-box attacks assume access to model parameters, activations, or gradients ( Nasr et al., 2019 ) , whereas black-box attacks operate under a more restrictive setting, relying exclusively on the model’s observable outputs ( Choquette-Choo et al., 2021 ) . Gray-box attacks occupy an intermediate threat model, granting access to quantities such as loss values or intermediate model states without requiring gradient-level information. In diffusion-model auditing, this distinction is often methodological: attacks that query intermediate denoising states generally assume local access to the model while avoiding the substantially greater computational cost of full white-box analysis. Most such query-based MIAs are threshold-based attacks : they define a continuous membership score 𝒮 θ ​ ( x ) \mathcal{S}_{\theta}(x) , such as reconstruction loss or prediction error, for a target model θ \theta and candidate sample x x , and classify the sample as a member when 𝒮 θ ​ ( x ) < τ {\mathcal{S}_{\theta}(x)<\tau} ( Yeom et al., 2018 ; Carlini et al., 2022 ) . The threshold τ \tau can be empirically calibrated to optimize attack performance, often subject to a desired False Positive Rate (FPR). More sophisticated attacks additionally use shadow models to calibrate the score distribution ( Shokri et al., 2017 ; Carlini et al., 2022 ) . MIAs on diffusion models. Auditing diffusion models requires analyzing the iterative denoising trajectory. While Carlini et al. (2022) achieved high precision with the Likelihood Ratio Attack (LiRA), their approach requires training numerous shadow models, making it computationally prohibitive. Consequently, efficient threshold-based attacks have become the standard. Matsumoto et al. (2023) introduced the Naive loss attack, which utilizes the diffusion training loss at specific timesteps as the membership score. To extract a more robust signal, Duan et al. (2023) proposed SecMI, which evaluates the reconstruction error along a deterministic trajectory via DDIM inversion, effectively isolating the membership signal from the high variance of stochastic forward noise. Kong et al. (2024) introduced the Proximal Initialization Attack (PIA), which initializes the forward process with a known deterministic noise vector near the clean data sample. PIA infers membership by evaluating the model’s noise estimation against this explicit ground-truth trajectory, achieving competitive accuracy with a reduced query budget. Finally, for conditional text-to-image models, Zhai et al. (2024) proposed CLiD, which measures the discrepancy between conditional and unconditional diffusion losses to expose memorization specific to the text-image pair. 3 Methodology 3.1 Preliminaries Generative trajectories and log-SNR. Full theoretical diagnostics and per-dataset results are provided in Appendix C.1 . 5 Conclusion We introduced difficulty calibration across two time axes to mitigate the image-difficulty confound in diffusion MIAs. Reference-Model Calibration (RMC) calibrates across training time using a pretrained checkpoint, while Temporal Self-Calibration (TSC) calibrates across diffusion time using the image’s own denoising trajectory. Experiments across diverse datasets, architectures, and training objectives demonstrate substantial gains in strict low-FPR membership detection. RMC enables near-perfect uncaptioned auditing of fine-tuned data, and TSC frequently doubles the TPR@1%FPR of the strongest trajectory-based baselines in fully unconstrained settings. Limitations and future work. Although our methods use only forward predictions and do not require gradients, they assume access to denoising outputs for candidate images at selected noise levels. This access may be unavailable through APIs that expose only final generated images, limiting direct application in such settings. RMC additionally assumes access to the checkpoint from which the audited model was fine-tuned. Its applicability is therefore restricted when this checkpoint is unavailable or the model’s training lineage is unknown. Future work could investigate whether related public checkpoints or ensembles of reference models can provide effective difficulty calibration in these cases. RMC measures loss changes between checkpoints and does not separately identify membership in the reference model’s pretraining corpus. Studying overlap between pretraining and fine-tuning data, and extending calibration across successive checkpoints, could clarify how membership evidence evolves across training stages. Ethics statement Membership inference has both privacy risks and legitimate auditing uses. Improved attacks could be misused to infer an individual’s participation in sensitive training data. At the same time, these methods can help individuals investigate whether their personal data were used to train or fine-tune diffusion models, and can support audits of candidate training-data sources for publicly released models, including those distributed through platforms such as Hugging Face. Such audits can help assess claims about dataset use and improve transparency around model provenance. Membership scores provide statistical evidence about candidate examples: a negative result does not prove that an example was excluded from training, and an audit does not identify a model’s complete training dataset.
